Buddy Guy's first Chess single, 'The First Time I Met the Blues,' was recorded March 6, 1960 at Chess Records, 2120 S. Michigan Ave.; he recorded for Chess from 1960 to 1967 and served as a house session guitarist for Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and others.

Spann was in constant demand as a Chess session pianist (Muddy Waters, Bo Diddley, Howlin' Wolf, Little Walter, Sonny Boy Williamson sessions); his 1954 single 'It Must Have Been the Devil' backed with 'Five Spot' was issued on Checker, the Chess subsidiary imprint.

Discogs documents a July 11, 1952 Chicago session released as 'Broken Heart' / 'Me and My Chauffeur' (as Memphis Minnie with Little Joe and His Band); her career bio lists Checker, a Chess subsidiary imprint, among the labels she recorded for (Columbia, Vocalion, Bluebird, OKeh, Regal, Checker, JOB).

EarlyBlues documents five Chess titles recorded by Elmore James plus a release on the Checker subsidiary; encyclopedia biographies confirm Chess among his recording labels.

The South Side Community Art Center opened December 15, 1940 with WPA Federal Art Project support and an inaugural exhibition of the movement's Black artists; it was the movement's visual-arts home, dedicated by Eleanor Roosevelt on May 7, 1941.

Sibling movement, held DISTINCT: Harlem's Renaissance was centered in New York in the 1920s; Chicago's flowered a decade later on the South Side, more working-class and politically radical, with its own institutions. The two are linked, never merged.

The Great Migration supplied the movement's people and subject: tens of thousands of Black Southerners reached Chicago's South Side, and its writers and artists turned that migration into literature, art, and scholarship.

Gwendolyn Brooks, the movement's poetic voice: A Street in Bronzeville (1945) and Annie Allen (1949), which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1950; a Hall Branch Book Review and Lecture Forum guest (1949 forum flyer, Harsh Collection).

Richard Wright, the movement's literary center: a South Side Writers Group member whose 'Blueprint for Negro Writing' is treated as the movement's central piece of literary theory, and whose Native Son (1940) defined its naturalism.
Lorraine Hansberry, raised in the movement's South Side world; her A Raisin in the Sun (graph era 1959) is staged here as the movement's late flowering.
Margaret Walker, South Side Writers Group member and movement poet (For My People), part of the Wright circle at the Abraham Lincoln Centre.

Katherine Dunham, dancer and choreographer named among the movement's artists in the standard accounts, formed in the same South Side institutional world.
